variants.title: Narrow the decision in stages
variants.context: A large recommender narrows the decision in stages: assemble request context, retrieve a candidate union, join compatible features, rank predicted value, construct a constrained slate, then log exposure and outcomes. Each stage has its own objective, budget, and failure mode.
variants.prompt: A home feed request arrives for a signed-in user. Put the pipeline stages in order.

items.text: Apply eligibility, deduplication, inventory, diversity, fatigue, and safety rules to construct the slate.
Retrieve a candidate union from embeddings, subscriptions, content, popularity, and bounded exploration with source identity.
Score the candidates with the production ranker inside a fixed latency and resource budget.
Load privacy-safe user state, recent intent, device, locale, surface, eligibility, and experiment assignment.
Join version-compatible user, item, context, and cross features under freshness and default contracts.
Log candidate sources, scores, positions, policy changes, probabilities, and later outcomes.

variants.hint: Each stage can only work on what the stage before it handed over.
variants.explanation: Retrieval owns recall, ranking owns precision, slate policy owns product constraints, and logging owns the evidence the next model will learn from.

variants.title: Narrow the decision in stages
variants.context: A large recommender narrows the decision in stages: assemble request context, retrieve a candidate union, join compatible features, rank predicted value, construct a constrained slate, then log exposure and outcomes. Each stage has its own objective, budget, and failure mode.
variants.prompt: A creator reports that a subscribed post never appeared for a follower. Put the trace steps in order.

items.text: Check whether the feature join produced stale values or silent defaults for it.
Check whether any retrieval source returned the post at all.
Check which slate policy rule removed, demoted, or deduplicated it.
Check the request context that was assembled, including surface eligibility and experiment assignment.
Check the exposure log for what was finally shown and in which position.
Check the score it received and which candidates outranked it.

variants.hint: A missing candidate cannot be a ranking bug.
variants.explanation: Debugging follows the same order as serving, because each stage can only be blamed for items that reached it.

variants.title: Narrow the decision in stages
variants.context: A large recommender narrows the decision in stages: assemble request context, retrieve a candidate union, join compatible features, rank predicted value, construct a constrained slate, then log exposure and outcomes. Each stage has its own objective, budget, and failure mode.
variants.prompt: A brand new item with no interaction history must have a path to exposure. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Log its selection probability so the delayed outcomes it earns can be used later.
Join its content features with defaults that mark the missing interaction history explicitly.
Assemble the request context and confirm surface, locale, and eligibility for this viewer.
Score it with the production ranker alongside established items.
Place it in the slate under the exploration and diversity limits the product allows.
Retrieve the item through content similarity and a bounded exploration quota rather than interaction history.

variants.hint: A cold item still has to be found before anything can score it.
variants.explanation: Cold start is a retrieval and policy problem first: without a retrieval path and an exploration quota, no ranker improvement can ever expose the item.

variants.title: Build a slate, not a sorted list
variants.context: A ranked pool is not a slate. Ranked candidates pass a fail-closed eligibility gate, a slate optimizer balances relevance against diversity, fatigue, inventory, and coverage across positions, and an exposure log stores the candidates, positions, probabilities, and policy decisions that produced the page.
variants.prompt: A ranked pool of 400 scored candidates must become a 12 position page. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Remove unsafe, unavailable, blocked, and region-ineligible items with a hard filter.
Take the ranked candidates with their scores, uncertainty, source identity, and model version.
Store the candidates, positions, probabilities, and policy decisions for later evaluation.
Balance relevance against diversity, novelty, fatigue, and source coverage across the positions.

variants.hint: One of these steps must never be traded off against relevance.
variants.explanation: Hard gates stay outside the learned objective so a violation can never be averaged away by a high relevance score.

variants.title: Build a slate, not a sorted list
variants.context: A ranked pool is not a slate. Ranked candidates pass a fail-closed eligibility gate, a slate optimizer balances relevance against diversity, fatigue, inventory, and coverage across positions, and an exposure log stores the candidates, positions, probabilities, and policy decisions that produced the page.
variants.prompt: One creator holds seven of the top ten scores for a viewer. Put the steps in order, ending with what makes the change auditable.

items.text: Eligibility removes anything blocked or unavailable before any coverage rule runs.
The optimizer enforces the creator cap and fills the freed positions from the remaining pool.
The ranker returns its scores with creator identity attached to each candidate.
The log records the pre-policy positions, the mutation, and the final positions.

variants.hint: Coverage rules operate on items that are already allowed to be shown.
variants.explanation: Recording the pre-policy and post-policy positions is what later lets evaluation separate model behavior from policy behavior.

variants.title: Build a slate, not a sorted list
variants.context: A ranked pool is not a slate. Ranked candidates pass a fail-closed eligibility gate, a slate optimizer balances relevance against diversity, fatigue, inventory, and coverage across positions, and an exposure log stores the candidates, positions, probabilities, and policy decisions that produced the page.
variants.prompt: The highest scoring candidate for a viewer is under a safety hold. Put the steps in order.

items.text: The eligibility gate drops it fail-closed rather than discounting its relevance.
The optimizer promotes the next eligible candidates and keeps the diversity floor.
The ranker scores it first, because affinity features know nothing about the hold.
The exposure log stores the removal reason alongside the slate that was served.

variants.hint: Ask whether a very high score should ever be allowed to buy an exception.
variants.explanation: Safety, legal, and inventory rules are hard gates, so the model never sees them as a cost it can outweigh.

variants.title: Budget the serving envelope
variants.context: Recommender capacity has separate drivers. Embedding storage is users plus items multiplied by dimensions, bytes per value, and replicas. Ranking work is candidates per request multiplied by traffic, sized against measured throughput at a safe utilization target. Slate policy budgets are counted in positions, not requests.
variants.prompt: A recommender stores embeddings for 20 million users and 5 million items at 256 dimensions with 4 bytes per value, held in 3 serving replicas. How much memory does the embedding set need?
variants.hint: Count the vectors first, then the bytes, then the copies.
variants.explanation: 25 million vectors times 256 dimensions is 6.4 billion values; at 4 bytes that is 25.6 GB per copy, and 3 replicas need 76.8 GB.

mistakes.feedback: 25.6 GB is one copy; replicas multiply the footprint and migrations can need overlap on top.
19.2 GB assumes one byte per value, but the stated representation is 4 bytes.

variants.title: Budget the serving envelope
variants.context: Recommender capacity has separate drivers. Embedding storage is users plus items multiplied by dimensions, bytes per value, and replicas. Ranking work is candidates per request multiplied by traffic, sized against measured throughput at a safe utilization target. Slate policy budgets are counted in positions, not requests.
variants.prompt: A ranker scores 550 candidates per request at 6,000 requests per second. One replica sustains 1,000,000 candidate scores per second and the team plans at a 60 percent utilization target. How many replicas does that require?
variants.hint: Ranking demand is candidates, not requests.
variants.explanation: Demand is 550 times 6,000, which is 3,300,000 candidate scores per second; safe capacity is 600,000 per replica; 3,300,000 divided by 600,000 is 5.5, rounded up to 6.

mistakes.feedback: 4 divides by the full 1,000,000 and ignores the 60 percent utilization target.
5 truncates 5.5 instead of rounding up and leaves half a replica of peak demand unplaced.

variants.title: Budget the serving envelope
variants.context: Recommender capacity has separate drivers. Embedding storage is users plus items multiplied by dimensions, bytes per value, and replicas. Ranking work is candidates per request multiplied by traffic, sized against measured throughput at a safe utilization target. Slate policy budgets are counted in positions, not requests.
variants.prompt: A surface serves 150,000 slates per hour with 12 positions each, and the policy reserves 10 percent of positions for bounded exploration. How many exploration slots exist per hour?
variants.hint: The reservation is written against positions, not against pages.
variants.explanation: 150,000 slates times 12 positions is 1,800,000 positions, and 10 percent of that is 180,000 exploration slots.

mistakes.feedback: 15,000 applies the 10 percent to slates, which is one exploration item per ten pages instead of per ten positions.
1,800,000 is every position on the surface, not the bounded share reserved for exploration.

variants.title: Judge a release by its evidence
variants.context: The current ranker decides what users can respond to, so its own logs are biased evidence. Releases are judged on negative signals, exposure distribution, and candidate-source contribution rather than on immediate clicks alone.
variants.prompt: A candidate ranker raises click-through by 4 percent while hides and skips rise and catalog coverage narrows. What should the release decide?
options: Promote it, because click-through is the surface's headline metric.
Hold it and weigh negative signals and exposure distribution before promoting.
Promote it to half of traffic and inspect retention next quarter.
optionFeedback: Clicks move with position, novelty, and selection effects, so a click gain alone is not evidence of a better product.
Correct: negative signals and exposure concentration are release evidence, not follow-up work.
Half of traffic is most of the harm, and a delayed look does not make the known regressions acceptable.
variants.hint: Ask which of the three observed changes were designed to be ignored.
variants.explanation: Promoting on click-through alone lets position and selection bias move a short-term number while users, suppliers, and the catalog get worse.

variants.title: Judge a release by its evidence
variants.context: The current ranker decides what users can respond to, so its own logs are biased evidence. Releases are judged on negative signals, exposure distribution, and candidate-source contribution rather than on immediate clicks alone.
variants.prompt: One retrieval source consumes 30 percent of the retrieval budget, and its items rarely survive into the final slate. What is the defensible move?
options: Measure its contribution after ranking and retire it if the slate never uses it.
Keep it, because removing a source always lowers recall at the candidate boundary.
Replace it with a popularity source, which is cheaper and always returns items.
optionFeedback: Correct: candidate-source contribution after ranking is what tells you an expensive source has no slate impact.
Recall at the boundary only matters for items the ranker and policy can actually use downstream.
Swapping in global popularity buys cheap candidates by narrowing exactly the coverage a union is meant to provide.
variants.hint: Which measurement is taken at the end of the pipeline rather than the start?
variants.explanation: Sources are evaluated by their contribution after ranking, so an expensive source with no effect on the served slate can be removed.

variants.title: Judge a release by its evidence
variants.context: The current ranker decides what users can respond to, so its own logs are biased evidence. Releases are judged on negative signals, exposure distribution, and candidate-source contribution rather than on immediate clicks alone.
variants.prompt: An embedding rebuild will leave part of the catalog on the previous generation for several hours. What is the correct handling?
options: Serve the mixed index, since most vectors already come from the new generation.
Keep serving the previous generation until the new one is complete and validated.
Compensate in ranking by boosting items that already have new-generation vectors.
optionFeedback: Distances between two embedding generations are not comparable, so a mixed index quietly corrupts neighbor sets.
Correct: backfills and rebuilds must not mix incompatible embedding generations on the serving path.
A boost hides the incompatibility behind a scoring change and biases exposure toward whatever was rebuilt first.
variants.hint: Ask whether two generations of vectors share a coordinate system.
variants.explanation: Index generations are published whole, because retrieval quality depends on every vector being comparable to every other vector.

variants.title: Match evidence to its source
variants.context: No single retrieval source, cold-start path, or feature family covers everything. Each one carries a different kind of evidence, which is why they are combined with source identity preserved instead of collapsed into one score.
variants.prompt: Match each retrieval family to the coverage it contributes to the candidate union.

pairs.label: Embedding neighbors
pairs.detail: Items close to a user, session, or query vector, limited by index recall and representation freshness.

pairs.label: Graph and subscriptions
pairs.detail: Follows, co-consumption, and item transitions that give high-precision relationship signals.

pairs.label: Content and rules
pairs.detail: Metadata, text, media, taxonomy, and locale matches that work when interactions are sparse.

pairs.label: Popularity and exploration
pairs.detail: Robust fallback and bounded evidence collection that must not consume the whole slate.

variants.hint: One family exists mainly so the others can be measured and replaced.
variants.explanation: A union with source quotas and preserved identity is what lets each source be measured, budgeted, and retired independently.

variants.title: Match evidence to its source
variants.context: No single retrieval source, cold-start path, or feature family covers everything. Each one carries a different kind of evidence, which is why they are combined with source identity preserved instead of collapsed into one score.
variants.prompt: Match each cold-start case to the evidence it can actually use.

pairs.label: New user
pairs.detail: A few high-information preference answers, context, and safe popularity until session behavior arrives.

pairs.label: Anonymous session
pairs.detail: Current intent, page context, locale, device, and short-lived state without inventing an identity.

pairs.label: New item
pairs.detail: Content embeddings, metadata, quality checks, supplier priors, and bounded exploration behind eligibility gates.

pairs.label: New market
pairs.detail: Compatible content and global priors that still need local language, policy, and inventory validation.

variants.hint: Ask what each case is missing and what it still has.
variants.explanation: Cold start is four different problems with different available evidence and risk, so one fallback path cannot serve all of them.

variants.title: Match evidence to its source
variants.context: No single retrieval source, cold-start path, or feature family covers everything. Each one carries a different kind of evidence, which is why they are combined with source identity preserved instead of collapsed into one score.
variants.prompt: Match each ranking feature family to what it carries into the score.

pairs.label: User features
pairs.detail: Stable preferences, recent interactions, frequency, negative feedback, and privacy-safe summaries.

pairs.label: Item features
pairs.detail: Content embeddings, freshness, quality, inventory, safety state, and calibrated popularity.

pairs.label: Context features
pairs.detail: Surface, device, time, locale, session intent, query, and experiment assignment.

pairs.label: Cross features
pairs.detail: User-item affinity, creator fatigue, novelty, sequence match, and prior exposure.

variants.hint: One family only exists when two others are joined.
variants.explanation: Feature families are versioned and joined point in time, so telemetry can tell a missing value apart from a delayed, defaulted, or intentionally absent one.
